title: Writing a PPX with ppxlib
body: A PPX is an OCaml program that receives the parsed syntax tree of your file, rewrites it, and hands the result back to the compiler. `ppxlib` provides the shared driver and a stable copy of the AST types, so one rewriter works across compiler versions. Extension points such as `[%shout "hello"]` are the simplest hook: the tree contains an `Pexp_extension` node and your rewriter replaces it.

You declare an extension with `Extension.V3.declare name context pattern expander`. The *pattern* (from `Ast_pattern`) describes the payload you accept, here a single string literal, and the *expander* receives the extracted string and returns a new expression built with `Ast_builder.Default`. Registering it with `Driver.register_transformation` makes it run when a project lists the rewriter in `(preprocess (pps ppx_shout))`.

Compile-time code is part of your trust boundary: it runs on every build. Keep rewriters small and deterministic, reject payloads you do not understand with a located error rather than a crash, and test them with expect tests that show the generated output.
challenge: The extension `[%shout "text"]` currently returns its string unchanged. Make the expander return the string in upper case so `[%shout "hello"]` becomes the literal "HELLO" at compile time.
projectInstructions: Run `dune test --root .`. The rewriter lives in ppx/ppx_shout.ml and the tests in test/shout_tests.ml use it through `(preprocess (pps ppx_shout ppx_expect))`. Edit only ppx/ppx_shout.ml.
question: When does the code inside a PPX rewriter run?
correct: At compile time, on the syntax tree, before the program is type checked
wrong: Only when the program raises an exception
reasoning: A PPX is a syntax-tree transformer run by the compiler driver, so its output is ordinary code that the type checker then sees.
